The wfx-loot campaign used 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to probe 61,764 repos and steal CI secrets and cloud credentials from at least 1,835 targets, then wiped its workflow runs in under a minute.

Aikido's research, via Bleeping Computer, shows a fast, automated CI/CD secrets grab that began around 12:45 UTC on November 10. Compromised accounts included some tied to Fortune 100 organizations, the US 🇺🇸 General Services Administration, the French 🇫🇷 government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO. About 50 appear to hold publishing rights on ecosystems like npm, PyPI, Go, crates, and Packagist.

- Access probe: the actor used the stolen credentials to open pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes" against repos each account could reach, testing for write access. 92% of those PRs are still open, so owners largely have not noticed.

- Payload delivery: a roughly 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script landed by modifying an existing GitHub Actions workflow, adding a new workflow on a short-lived branch, or planting an npm install hook.

- What it harvests: Actions secrets and variables, the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, AWS, Azure and Google Cloud credentials (including instance metadata on self-hosted runners), plus Git, SSH, GPG, Docker, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, Vault and Terraform creds. It also targets AI tool keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Hugging Face, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, along with .env files, private keys, keystores, shell histories, process memory, recent commits and workflow artifacts.

- Cloud escalation and persistence: the script exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure and GCP sessions. In AWS it can chain into other IAM roles found in the repo to create long-lived credentials for IAM users, and it uses service-account credentials to impersonate identities in GCP. Where permissions allow, it can modify cloud identity and trust policies.

- Exfil and cleanup: data was tarballed and sent by HTTP POST to one of two attacker-controlled endpoints. The actor then reverted its changes and deleted workflow runs and logs in under a minute. Automated publishing carried the payload into Packagist digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and Go module github[.]com/onuragtas/docker-env v1.0.278 and v1.0.280. Researchers see the package releases as a byproduct of automated publishing, with CI secrets the main goal, and note overlap with the 2025 GhostAction campaign.

Takeaway: because the actor deleted runs and logs, the residue matters. Check your repos for the wfx-docs branch, the "docs: dependency audit notes" probe PR, and gaps in workflow run numbers. Review workflow files and npm install hooks for unexpected changes. If payload execution is confirmed, treat every secret and cloud role available to those workflows as compromised and rotate immediately, then review cloud IAM and trust policies for new long-lived credentials. The report does not list the two exfil endpoints or detection rules.

Microsoft, 11 Nov: two studies on post-training supply chain attacks against coding agents. Dataset poisoning with 90 crafted examples in 9,000 conversations reached 78% attack success; model poisoning of an open-weight checkpoint reached 84-95% on unseen repos. The trigger is an ordinary user request, so prompt-injection filters see nothing. Which open-weight checkpoints do you run, and who signed them?

Researchers planted one file in a Downloads folder: AGENTS.md.

When Codex read it, it added a malicious MCP server to its machine-wide config in more than 90% of attempts. Claude Code followed a similar CLAUDE.md about 50% of the time.

Their conclusion: there is nothing to patch. The agents did exactly what they were built to do.

Coding agents treat every file they read as instructions. Test what your agents can read, not just what they write.

Speaking at @aiDotEngineer Code Summit SF, the "software factory stack" seemed to resonate. Here's a breakdown of the components:

00 – Factories-as-code. Every aspect of the factory (agent workflows, access permissions, cloud sandbox configuration, and so on) should be version-controlled code that humans and agents can modify.

01 – Data & Context. You should own all of the data your agent interacts with on your own infrastructure. Your internal skills and MCPs, agent traces, access logs, telemetry... everything.

02 – Compute. Agents should have their own computer, with controlled sandbox permissions and support for multiple operating systems. This should be self-hostable.

03 – Inference. You should have access to any model and any harness to benchmark the right match for your setup. Don't lock in to any one model provider.

04 – Improvement. You (and agents) need tools to measure and improve your factory. This means observability over cost-per-PR, cycle times, latency, and other DORA metrics. It also means self-improvement, with agents scoring output quality, proposing changes to the factory, and re-measuring in a loop.

05 – Orchestration. You need a runtime to launch agents, track work, and recover from failures. It should also handle message passing between agents in a multi-agent system.

06 – Access. You should be able to connect the factory to any external system. You'll want an MCP server and REST API to access the factory itself, and integrations with where your team works (Slack, MS Teams, Jira, Linear, etc). We don't recommend an "ADE" or web interface that's tightly coupled to the factory.

A longer CLAUDE.md can make Claude Code do worse work. Every line should stop a mistake you've seen.

1. The AWS Bedrock slip one line fixed

2. Why to trim /init's draft

3. Who wins when two files disagree

4. What importing AGENTS.md costs

5. The test for every line

🧵

Your coding agent can edit CLAUDE.md.

So every rule in it is one the agent can quietly rewrite, in a PR you skim.

Keep the rule files out of its reach. One deny list in .claude/settings.json and Claude Code refuses the edit.

A rule your agent can edit is a suggestion. https://t.co/UzDOycU1qG

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/CLAUDE.md look almost the same, but in Claude Code they have opposite effects on AGENTS.md.

The first one changes nothing, while the second turns it off in every project under your home folder.

Let me explain what I found so far:

Claude Code /doctor prompt-audit [path] is a great idea. 🔍

It audits your AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, skills, and other agent instructions for outdated or contradictory guidance in your repositorie.

We review our code. We should review the instructions guiding our AI agents too. 🧹

Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents（プライベートベータ）。

利用層拡大の一手。リスク回避で及び腰だったところに差し込める。

・エージェントのハーネス・サンドボックス・セッション履歴を、自社クラウドまたはオンプレミスで完全ホスト可能

・コードベースや内部システムへのアクセスを伴う業務（ビルド修正、アラートトリアージなど）を、セキュリティ境界内で安全に実行

・Claudeへのモデル呼び出し先を、Anthropic / Bedrock / Agent Platform / Foundryなどから選択可能

・対象組織限定のプライベートベータ。

・Anthropicアカウントチーム経由でアクセスをリクエスト

データ主権とガバナンスを確保したまま、本番環境でエージェントを動かせる形になりますね。

Claude Code と Codex を並列で動かすなら、worktree は入れておきたい。

でも筆者の環境では、worktree を入れても事故が4つ起きました。

何が防げて、何が防げないのか。5つの決まりにまとめました🧵
#ClaudeCode #AIエージェント https://t.co/QmBMeFtCwx

claude's login broke for about an hour this morning. https://t.co/B2smzA8X2r and claude code both

if your whole workday runs through one agent, set this up before the next one:

1. an API key fallback. claude code can run on ANTHROPIC_API_KEY instead of your subscription login
2. a second agent already installed and signed in
3. your rules in AGENTS.md, imported from CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md, so both tools read the same instructions
4. commit before every long agent run so a dropped session doesn't eat half a change
5. a bookmarked status page so you know it's them and not your wifi

microsoft 365 was down for 12+ hours yesterday too. one tool is one point of failure

vercel's workflow sdk 4 took 21 min to finish a 1,020 step run. sdk 5 does it in 3

the steps are 1 KB of json, no model anywhere. those 18 min were the durability layer replaying its own log and hopping queues

how many "the model is slow" complaints are actually this?
